title: T-Cell Defects: Age-Specific Counts, 22q11.2 Deletion, Bare Lymphocyte Syndromes and Wiskott-Aldrich
summary: Learn why lymphocyte counts must be read against age-specific intervals, how 22q11.2 deletion, MHC class II and class I deficiency, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and IPEX break T-cell development or function, and which lab test points to each.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 52 Hit 2 (lymphocyte count and T-cell deficiency), Hit 7 (Wiskott-Aldrich), Hit 8 (22q11.2 deletion and IPEX), Hit 9 (bare lymphocyte syndromes I and II) and Trap 4 (BLS II spares the MHC genes), checked against Dvorak 2023 (PIDTC 2022 definitions; read via a page-fetch tool), Zhang 2022 (paediatric lymphocyte reference values), Biggs 2023 (22q11.2), Lum 2019 (MHC class II deficiency), Haskologlu 2025 (MHC class I deficiency), Buchbinder 2014, Hosahalli Vasanna 2021 and Jin 2019 (Wiskott-Aldrich) and Gambineri 2018 and Ben-Skowronek 2021 (IPEX). Hit 2’s fixed “<1200/mm³” threshold and “normal >1500 at any age” ignore age-specific intervals (register flag rv-lymphocyte-threshold-age); the naïve CD4 <200 cut-off and the 1200 threshold are not taught. Hit 7’s “IgA high, IgM low” and “only WAS has small platelets” are qualified (register flag rv-was-microplatelets-ig-pattern). Hit 9’s “decreased CD8+” is qualified: total CD8 can be preserved (register flag rv-mhc1-cd8-naive). Hit 8’s IPEX “death within 2 years unless treated” is pending. Trap 4 is confirmed by Lum 2019.

objectives: Interpret lymphocyte and T-cell counts against age-specific reference intervals rather than a single adult threshold.
Distinguish 22q11.2 deletion, MHC class II deficiency, MHC class I deficiency, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and IPEX by mechanism and key laboratory finding.
Explain why bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is caused by defects in transcription regulators, not in the MHC class II genes.

scenes.title: Three children, three T-cell puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three children referred to immunology — (1) a 5-month-old with Pneumocystis pneumonia and chronic diarrhoea, an absolute lymphocyte count of 2,000/µL that the ward calls “normal”, very low CD4 cells and an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio; (2) a 2-year-old boy with eczema, bruising and a platelet count of 25 × 10⁹/L, first labelled immune thrombocytopenia; (3) a newborn with tetralogy of Fallot, low calcium and a low TREC result on the newborn screen. Question token: “Which defect, and which test?”

cues.text: Three children. A five-month-old with Pneumocystis pneumonia and chronic diarrhoea, whose lymphocyte count of two thousand was called normal, but whose CD4 cells are very low.
A two-year-old boy with eczema, bruising and a very low platelet count. And a newborn with a heart defect, low calcium and a low TREC screen.
Which defect does each child have, and which lab test points to it?

scenes.title: Where T cells are made and taught
scenes.altText: Schematic: the thymus as a school for T cells. The thymus develops from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. Inside, MHC class II molecules on thymic epithelium select CD4 T cells, and MHC class I molecules select CD8 T cells. MHC class I needs the TAP transporter to carry peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, and presents them to CD8 T cells and NK cells. Count card: lymphocyte counts change with age — in one reference study of healthy Chinese children, total lymphocytes peaked in infancy (2–12 months: median 4,498/µL, 2.5th percentile 2,309/µL) and fell later (7–18 years: median 2,043/µL, 2.5th percentile 1,226/µL).

cues.text: T cells are made in the thymus, which grows from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches of the embryo. Each new T cell carries a TREC, a marker of fresh thymic output.
In the thymus, MHC class two molecules select CD4 helper cells, and MHC class one molecules select CD8 cells.
MHC class one needs a peptide pump called TAP to load its peptides, and then shows them to CD8 T cells and NK cells.
Normal counts depend on age. In one reference study, lymphocytes peaked in infancy, with a lower limit of about two thousand three hundred per microlitre, and fell in older children.

scenes.title: Four ways the T-cell school fails
scenes.altText: Four cards and a token. 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge): about 1 in 4,000 births; abnormal third/fourth pharyngeal pouches give heart defects, hypoparathyroidism and a small or absent thymus; complete athymia in under 1.5% (needs thymus transplant); most have partial DiGeorge with mild-to-moderate T-cell lymphopenia that improves, and mitogen responses are usually normal. MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II): autosomal recessive; the MHC locus itself is intact — mutations are in the transcription regulators CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP and RFXANK (over 85% in the RFX complex, about half RFXANK); severe CD4 lymphopenia with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, hypogammaglobulinaemia, absent specific antibody; severe viral infections; untransplanted mean age at death about 4 years. MHC class I deficiency (type I): TAP1, TAP2, tapasin (TAPBP) or β2-microglobulin defects; HLA-ABC typically 1–15% of normal; total CD8 may be preserved while naïve CD8 cells are markedly reduced; recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, bronchiectasis and granulomatous skin lesions from childhood or adolescence. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: X-linked WAS gene; microthrombocytopenia, eczema, combined immunodeficiency; mild variant X-linked thrombocytopenia (XLT) from the same gene. Token: IPEX = FOXP3, X-linked, loss of regulatory T cells, onset usually in the first months.

cues.text: A 22q11.2 deletion, DiGeorge syndrome, affects about one in four thousand births. Faulty pharyngeal pouches give heart defects, low calcium and a small thymus. Fewer than one and a half percent have no thymus at all; most have mild to moderate T-cell lymphopenia that improves.

Bare lymphocyte syndrome type two is MHC class two deficiency, but the MHC genes are intact. The mutations hit four transcription regulators: CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP and RFXANK. CD4 cells fall, the CD4 to CD8 ratio inverts, and antibodies are low.

Type one is MHC class one deficiency, usually from TAP1 or TAP2 defects. Total CD8 counts can be normal, though naive CD8 cells are reduced. Patients typically get lung infections, bronchiectasis and granulomatous skin lesions later in childhood.
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is X-linked: small platelets with thrombocytopenia, eczema and combined immunodeficiency. A milder form of the same gene, X-linked thrombocytopenia, mainly affects platelets.
And IPEX: FOXP3 mutations remove regulatory T cells, with autoimmunity usually starting in the first months of life.

scenes.title: Which test for which defect
scenes.altText: Test cards. Counts: interpret T-cell and lymphocyte counts against age-specific reference intervals (PIDTC 2022); its age-specific low-T-cell cutoffs are under 0.6 × 10⁹/L at any age, under 0.8 if aged 2–4 years, under 1.0 if younger than 2 years; typical SCID includes fewer than 20% naïve CD4 cells (CD45RA) or low TRECs. MHC class II deficiency: flow cytometry shows absent or very low HLA-DR on lymphocytes; TREC can be normal, so newborn screening can miss it. MHC class I deficiency: low HLA-ABC on flow cytometry; gene testing for TAP1/TAP2. Wiskott-Aldrich: flow cytometry for intracellular WASp as a rapid screen, then WAS gene sequencing; MPV usually under 5 fL, but microplatelets were found in only about half of patients in one large series. 22q11.2 deletion: FISH detects about 95% (misses some nested deletions); MLPA or microarray. Hook answers: (1) MHC class II deficiency — HLA-DR flow; (2) Wiskott-Aldrich — WASp flow and WAS gene; (3) 22q11.2 deletion — FISH or MLPA, with naïve T-cell phenotyping.

cues.text: Start with the count, read against age-specific intervals. The 2022 SCID definitions set lower T-cell cutoffs for younger children, and look at naive CD4 cells and TRECs.
MHC class two deficiency shows absent or very low HLA-DR on lymphocytes by flow cytometry. TRECs can be normal, so newborn screening can miss it. Class one deficiency shows low HLA-ABC.

For Wiskott-Aldrich, flow cytometry for the WAS protein inside cells is a rapid screen, and gene sequencing confirms. For a 22q11.2 deletion, FISH finds about ninety-five percent, and MLPA or microarray catches more.
Back to the hook. The infant has MHC class two deficiency: check HLA-DR. The boy needs WAS protein testing. The newborn needs testing for a 22q11.2 deletion, with naive T-cell counts.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is caused by mutations in MHC class II genes” (✓ the MHC locus is intact; the defects are in CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP or RFXANK); “A lymphocyte count of 2,000/µL in a 4-month-old is normal” (✓ infant intervals are higher — in one study the 2–12-month lower limit was about 2,300/µL); “Normal-sized platelets rule out Wiskott-Aldrich” (✓ microplatelets were present in only about half of one large series; XLT, from the same gene, also has thrombocytopenia).

cues.text: Trap one: bare lymphocyte syndrome type two is a mutation in the MHC class two genes. No: those genes are intact. The regulators that switch them on are broken.
Trap two: a lymphocyte count of two thousand in a four-month-old is normal. No: infants run much higher, so compare with an age-specific interval.
Trap three: normal-sized platelets rule out Wiskott-Aldrich. No: small platelets were seen in only about half of patients in one large series.

scenes.title: School, printer, scaffold
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The thymus is the SCHOOL (22q11.2 deletion = a small or missing school); MHC molecules are the textbooks, and bare lymphocyte syndrome type II has a broken PRINTER (CIITA/RFX regulators), not bad textbook files (MHC genes); WASp is the actin SCAFFOLD, so without it platelets come out wee.” Tokens: School = thymus · Printer = CIITA/RFX · Scaffold = WASp. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: school, printer, scaffold. The thymus is the school; a 22q11.2 deletion leaves it small. In bare lymphocyte syndrome type two the MHC textbook files are fine, but the printer, the CIITA and RFX regulators, is broken. WAS protein is the actin scaffold; without it platelets come out small.

Where it breaks: most children with the deletion still have some thymus and improve; in class one deficiency total CD8 counts can be normal; and small platelets are missing in about half of Wiskott-Aldrich patients.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Counts: age-specific intervals · 22q11.2: most partial · BLS II: CIITA/RFX, not MHC genes”, “MHC class I: CD8 may be normal · WAS: small platelets in about half”.

cues.text: Read inherited T-cell defects by mechanism and age: compare lymphocyte counts with age-specific intervals, remember that bare lymphocyte syndrome type II breaks the regulators of intact MHC class II genes, that MHC class I deficiency can leave total CD8 counts normal, and that Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome often but not always shows small platelets.

props.label: Age-specific counts · 22q11.2 mostly partial · BLS II = CIITA/RFX
MHC class I: total CD8 may be normal · WAS: small platelets in ~half

explanation.what: Plain language: T cells are trained in the thymus and learn to recognise antigen shown on MHC molecules. Some children are born with a small thymus, with cells that cannot switch on their MHC molecules, or with a broken cytoskeleton protein, and each problem leaves its own fingerprint in the lab. Scientific terms: T-cell lymphopenia, age-specific reference intervals, naïve CD4 (CD45RA) T cells, TREC, 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome), congenital athymia, MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II; CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP, RFXANK), MHC class I deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type I; TAP1, TAP2, TAPBP, B2M), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS gene, WASp), X-linked thrombocytopenia (XLT), microthrombocytopenia, mean platelet volume (MPV), IPEX (FOXP3, regulatory T cells).
explanation.why: MHC class II on thymic epithelium is needed to select CD4 T cells, so without it CD4 counts fall and T-cell help for antibody fails. MHC class I selects CD8 T cells, but in class I deficiency other T-cell populations expand and total CD8 counts can be preserved. Pharyngeal pouch maldevelopment in 22q11.2 deletion shrinks the thymus. WASp links receptor signalling to actin, so loss of WASp affects lymphocytes and platelet formation. FOXP3 is needed for regulatory T cells, so its loss unleashes autoimmunity.
explanation.measure: Lymphocyte and T-cell counts against age-specific intervals (one study: lymphocytes 2,309–7,003/µL at 2–12 months, 1,226–4,767/µL at 7–18 years; PIDTC 2022 low-T-cell cutoffs <0.6 × 10⁹/L at any age, <0.8 at 2–4 years, <1.0 under 2 years); naïve CD4 proportion and TREC; flow cytometry for HLA-DR (absent in MHC class II deficiency) and HLA-ABC (typically 1–15% of normal in class I deficiency); intracellular WASp flow cytometry and WAS sequencing; MPV (usually <5 fL in WAS, normal 7.2–11.7 fL in one review); FISH (about 95% detection), MLPA or microarray for 22q11.2.
explanation.differs: MHC class II deficiency (low CD4, inverted ratio, hypogammaglobulinaemia, severe viral infections in infancy) vs MHC class I deficiency (CD8 may be normal, bronchiectasis and granulomatous skin lesions later in childhood); complete DiGeorge (athymia, <1.5%) vs partial (mild-to-moderate lymphopenia that improves); classic WAS (absent WASp) vs XLT (residual WASp, milder); WAS (small platelets in about half) vs immune thrombocytopenia (larger platelets on average).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the gene class behind BLS II (CIITA/RFX regulators, not MHC genes), the classic WAS triad, the 22q11.2 triad of heart defect, hypocalcaemia and thymic hypoplasia, or why an infant lymphocyte count must be compared with an age-specific range.

mnemonic.text: School, printer, scaffold: the thymus is the SCHOOL (small in 22q11.2 deletion); in bare lymphocyte syndrome type II the MHC textbook files are fine but the PRINTER (CIITA/RFX regulators) is broken; WASp is the actin SCAFFOLD, so without it platelets come out wee.
mnemonic.explanation: Ties each defect to the structure that fails: organ, gene regulation or cytoskeleton.
mnemonic.limitation: Most children with 22q11.2 deletion still have some thymus and improve; in MHC class I deficiency total CD8 counts can be normal; small platelets are absent in about half of Wiskott-Aldrich patients, and XLT from the same gene is milder.

The lymphocyte reference values come from one study of healthy Chinese children on one platform; laboratories must use their own age-specific intervals.
takeaway: Read inherited T-cell defects by mechanism and age: compare lymphocyte counts with age-specific intervals, remember that bare lymphocyte syndrome type II breaks the regulators of intact MHC class II genes, that MHC class I deficiency can leave total CD8 counts normal, and that Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome often but not always shows small platelets.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old has Pneumocystis pneumonia and chronic diarrhoea. Flow cytometry shows very low CD4 T cells with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio, and HLA-DR is absent on B cells; immunoglobulins are low. Which genetic finding is most likely?

options.text: Biallelic mutations in RFXANK, a regulator of MHC class II transcription
options.rationale: Correct. This is MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II); the MHC locus is intact and over 85% of cases involve the RFX complex, about half RFXANK.

options.text: A mutation in the HLA-DRB1 gene on chromosome 6
options.rationale: Incorrect. In MHC class II deficiency the MHC genes themselves are intact; the defect is in the transcription regulators CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP or RFXANK.
Incorrect. TAP defects cause MHC class I deficiency, with low HLA-ABC, not absent HLA-DR, and usually present later with bronchiectasis.
Incorrect. The 22q11.2 deletion reduces thymic tissue but does not remove HLA-DR from B cells.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has an absolute lymphocyte count of 2,000/µL. A colleague calls it normal because it is above 1,500/µL. What is the best response?

options.text: Compare it with an age-specific interval; infant lymphocyte counts run higher, so this may be low
options.rationale: Correct. Lymphocyte and T-cell counts are interpreted against age-associated reference intervals; in one reference study the lower limit at 2–12 months was about 2,300/µL.

options.text: Agree; any count above 1,500/µL is normal at every age
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lymphocyte counts peak in infancy and fall with age, so an adult-style threshold can miss infant lymphopenia.

options.text: Agree; T-cell deficiency is only suspected below 1,200/µL
options.rationale: Incorrect. A single fixed threshold ignores age; the PIDTC 2022 definitions use age-specific T-cell cutoffs and naïve T-cell measures.

options.text: Lymphocyte counts cannot be interpreted before 2 years of age
options.rationale: Incorrect. Age-specific reference intervals exist from birth, and newborn TREC screening relies on early assessment.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent ear infections and thrombocytopenia. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is suspected. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Flow cytometry for intracellular WAS protein is a rapid screen, and WAS gene sequencing confirms
options.rationale: Correct. Flow-cytometric WASp quantification is recommended as a screen in suspected WAS, followed by sequencing of the WAS gene.

options.text: A normal mean platelet volume rules out Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. Microplatelets were found in only about half of patients in one large series, and normal or even large platelets have been reported.

options.text: Boys and girls are affected equally
options.rationale: Incorrect. WAS is X-linked and manifests in males; affected females are rare.

options.text: Megakaryocytes are usually absent from the marrow
options.rationale: Incorrect. Megakaryocyte numbers are typically normal; platelet formation is abnormal.

claims.text: Lymphocyte and T-cell counts must be read against age-specific intervals; infant counts run higher (one study: 2–12 months 2,309–7,003/µL; 7–18 years 1,226–4,767/µL); PIDTC 2022 age-specific T-cell cutoffs and naïve CD4/TREC criteria.
Reviewer Hit 2: absolute lymphocyte count <1200/mm³ suggests T-cell deficiency; normal >1500/mm³ at any age; naïve CD4 <200 suggests severe T-cell deficiency.
claims.note: Not taught as rules; no open source read in this session gives these thresholds, and age-specific intervals contradict a single “any age” normal (register flag rv-lymphocyte-threshold-age).

claims.text: 22q11.2 deletion: ~1 in 4,000; pharyngeal pouch defects; complete athymia <1.5%; most partial with mild-to-moderate T lymphopenia that improves; normal mitogen responses; FISH ~95%, MLPA/microarray.
MHC class II deficiency: MHC genes intact; CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP, RFXANK; low CD4, inverted ratio, hypogammaglobulinaemia; absent HLA-DR; TREC can be normal.
MHC class I deficiency: TAP1/TAP2/TAPBP/B2M; HLA-ABC 1–15% of normal; total CD8 may be preserved, naïve CD8 reduced; bronchiectasis and granulomatous skin lesions in later childhood.

WAS: X-linked; microthrombocytopenia, eczema, combined immunodeficiency; XLT from the same gene; WASp flow screen and sequencing; MPV usually <5 fL but microplatelets in only about half; megakaryocytes normal; variable immunoglobulin pattern.
IPEX: X-linked FOXP3 defect, loss of regulatory T cells, onset usually in the first months; enteropathy, type 1 diabetes, eczema.
Reviewer Hit 8: IPEX causes death within 2 years unless treated.
claims.note: Not taught; the sources read describe poor outcomes and HSCT as treatment of choice but do not give this figure clearly.

claims.text: Scenario invented; thymus, MHC and cells schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 52 Hit 2 gives a fixed absolute lymphocyte threshold (<1200/mm³) and says normal is >1500/mm³ “at any age”. Lymphocyte counts are strongly age-dependent: in Zhang 2022 the 2.5th percentile at 2–12 months was 2,309/µL, and the PIDTC 2022 definitions (Dvorak 2023) require interpretation against age-associated intervals with age-specific T-cell cutoffs and give no absolute lymphocyte count threshold (register flag rv-lymphocyte-threshold-age).

Ch. 52 Hit 7 says “IgA high, IgM low” and “only WAS has small platelets”. Microplatelets were present in only 53% of the Sullivan series (Hosahalli Vasanna 2021) and some patients have normal or large platelets (Jin 2019); XLT, from the same gene, also causes thrombocytopenia (Jin 2019 found lower MPV in WAS/XLT than in ITP); the immunoglobulin pattern is variable (Buchbinder 2014: IgG, IgM and IgA often low, IgE high; Jin 2019: IgA raised in 36%, IgM low in 39%) (register flag rv-was-microplatelets-ig-pattern).

Ch. 52 Hit 9 says MHC class I deficiency causes “decreased CD8+”. Haskologlu 2025 reports that total CD8 counts may be preserved while naïve CD8 cells are markedly reduced (CD8 low in 3 of 11 cohort patients), and lists TAPBP and B2M as further causes beyond TAP1/TAP2 (register flag rv-mhc1-cd8-naive).

morphology.note: No micrographs; thymus, MHC molecules, cells and tests are shown as schematic cards.

verification.notes: Six factual claims checked against Dvorak 2023 (read via a page-fetch tool), Zhang 2022, Biggs 2023, Lum 2019, Haskologlu 2025, Buchbinder 2014, Hosahalli Vasanna 2021, Jin 2019, Gambineri 2018 and Ben-Skowronek 2021 (Europe PMC full text). Two reviewer claims (fixed lymphocyte/naïve CD4 thresholds; IPEX death within 2 years) are pending and not taught. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
